Every spring, the town repainted the bench beside the bus stop. Every summer, the paint peeled.

No one knew who had built the bench. Its legs were uneven, and rain gathered in the shallow groove along its seat. The council discussed replacing it with something sturdier, but never did. People kept using it while they waited: schoolchildren swinging their feet, shoppers resting their bags, an old man who came on Tuesdays though he never boarded a bus.

One year, someone sanded the seat before painting it. Someone else cut a narrow channel so the rain could run off. By autumn, the bench was still blue.

The old man noticed first. He put down his newspaper and ran his palm across the dry wood. Then the bus arrived, and everyone stood.
